oba.reading_mnemonic: As the cats bolt, she cries <reading>Oh, baa!</reading> — sheep noise, not sheep, just her own flustered yelp. That startled cry, <reading>おば</reading>, is the exact sound of an aunt arriving at Grandma Kane's shrine every single year, scarf and all.
oba.description: The vowel here is short — don't stretch it into the longer sound used for the word for grandmother. They look and sound almost identical on the page but name different relatives, so lean on the mnemonic's short, startled yelp to keep the vowel length honest.

obaasan.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank where the washing happens, an old woman scrubs scarves for the whole village and refuses anyone's help. Children stop to greet her properly before crossing, and she waves them on with damp hands. To everyone nearby, respectfully, she's simply grandmother — polite, warm, and impossible to argue with.
obaasan.reading_mnemonic: おばあさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おばあさん</reading> read straight through.
obaasan.description: おばあさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly woman, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "ma'am" than a strict family term.

ocha.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she pours something pale green and steaming into small cups for every visitor who climbs the mossy steps, cats sniffing at the tray. One sip after the climb and you understand why she never skips this step: tea.
ocha.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hot can rolls off the shelf and lands right at your feet, steam still hissing from the seam. You yelp <reading>oh, cha!</reading> as it burns your fingers picking it up. That yelp is the reading: <reading>おちゃ</reading>.
ocha.description: Almost always appears with the honorific prefix お attached — daily speech rarely uses the bare form alone, even though it exists in other compounds.

oji.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the point where most people turn back, a man in hiking boots is refilling the lone vending machine himself — turns out it's your uncle, who apparently owns the machine and hikes up every week just to restock it. Nobody in the family questions this anymore. That's just what your uncle does.
oji.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker rounds the last switchback and yelps, oh, gee, at the stranger already there. It's not a stranger — it's your uncle, and that startled gasp is exactly <reading>おじ</reading>: <reading>oh, gee</reading>, uncle, fancy meeting you up here.
oji.description: 叔父 marks a younger uncle — your parent's younger brother, or one married in — as distinct from the term for an older uncle, though both get shortened to the same casual address form in speech.

ojiisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the old bell-ringer finally hands the rope to someone new: a stooped man with a walking stick who has swept the mossy steps every morning for forty years. The cats accept him instantly. The children bow and call him grandfather, and from that day the enormous bell is his alone to ring.
ojiisan.reading_mnemonic: おじいさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おじいさん</reading> read straight through.
ojiisan.description: おじいさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly man, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "grandpa" than a strict family term.

okaasan.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a boy collapses by the lone vending machine, certain he can't take one more step. Then his mother crests the rise behind him, unbothered, carrying his backpack, her water bottle, and a spare pair of socks, somehow not out of breath. That endless, unglamorous readiness is what mother (polite) means.
okaasan.reading_mnemonic: Driving the mountain trail's last hairpin toward the vending machine at the top, she doesn't slow down. The kids in the back seat brace and yell <reading>oh, car, san</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>おかあさん</reading> sounds, screamed by children who have done this drive with her before.

okusan.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, a woman leans against the lone vending machine, patient in the shade of an oak, clearly waiting for somebody. Every exhausted hiker who finally staggers up assumes she must belong to whoever shows up gasping right after — and that assumption, someone waiting up there for her other half, is exactly (someone's) wife.
okusan.reading_mnemonic: She waves at the oak baking in the noon sun and calls down the trail, <reading>oak sun</reading> — the greeting that carries all the way to the switchbacks. That call is just how <reading>おくさん</reading> sounds: someone's wife, waiting patiently at the top for him to catch up.
okusan.description: 奥さん is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's wife — never your own. It also gets used casually to address a married woman in general, but it is not what a man calls his own wife.

onaka.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a man buys every onigiri on the shelf and eats them standing at the counter, one after another, until his shirt stops closing. By the last one his middle has ballooned into a round drum he has to hold with both hands — his stomach, full past reason, the only thing left worth talking about.
onaka.reading_mnemonic: Koichi watches the man's belly swell round as a spare tire and mutters he looks like he's got one strapped <reading>on a car</reading>. The man just groans <reading>おなか</reading>, patting the bulge, and Koichi decides that's as good a name for it as any.

oneesan.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the captain of the school relay team, the one every younger kid looks up to and never dares call by her first name. She lines up the little ones, ties their shoelaces, and lets them win. That respectful, polite way you address someone's honored older sister is exactly this word.
oneesan.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, the team captain warms up by impersonating a horse, letting out an exaggerated <reading>neigh</reading> before every sprint. The younger kids salute her respectfully as <reading>おねえさん</reading>, the neighing captain, and nobody questions it.
oneesan.description: This word is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's older sister, or an unrelated older woman as a term of respect — it is not the plain, private term you'd use among your own family growing up with a younger sibling.

oniisan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a young man rings the enormous bell for an elderly stranger who can't reach the rope, then carries her offering up the mossy steps himself while the shrine cats trail behind them. Nobody there is related to him, but everyone calls him older brother (polite) anyway, because that is simply what the word is for.
oniisan.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats climb his leg the moment he sits on the mossy steps, and he winces <reading>oh, knee, sahn</reading> as claws land — which is exactly how <reading>おにいさん</reading> sounds, and exactly why the cats never leave him alone.
oniisan.description: The polite, respectful form used to talk about or address someone else's older brother, or a young man in general as a courteous form of address — contrast with the plain word used only for your own older brother.

onnanohito.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> finally rises from her bow and falls into step beside the two legs she already knows as a <kanji>person</kanji>, the pair of them striding together past the cats toward the enormous bell. Kneeling figure plus striding legs, moving as one down the mossy steps — that's a grown woman.
onnanohito.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのひと</reading>.

onnanoko.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a tiny figure copies the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> pose out on the sports field, except her sweeping arm has curled inward to cradle a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, little arms flung out against her chest. A pint-sized woman who still has a bundled baby's shape tucked in her arms — that's a girl.
onnanoko.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのこ</reading>.

otokonohito.meaning_mnemonic: Out in the paddy, the <kanji>man</kanji> finally straightens up from the plow, gives his arm one last flex, and starts walking toward Koichi's konbini for something cold — those two legs carrying him off the field are exactly the <kanji>person</kanji> he becomes the second he stops working. Power in the field, then legs on the road: that's a grown man.
otokonohito.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのひと</reading>.

otokonoko.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, a small figure flexes one arm at the vending machine exactly like the <kanji>man</kanji> dragging his plow through the paddy, except his other arm is still tucked into a <kanji>child</kanji>'s swaddle, wriggling loose at his side. A miniature man who hasn't finished unwrapping yet — that's a boy.
otokonoko.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのこ</reading>.

otona.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward suddenly stops and throws their arms out wide, legs spread as far as they'll go — the stance for showing off something <kanji>big</kanji>. Nobody teaches a kid to stand like that; you grow into needing the room. Standing tall enough to need the whole stance is what makes you an adult.
otona.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby stops wailing the second someone hands him <reading>a tuna</reading> — the calm is instant, like a switch. Jin ducks through the doorway just in time to see it: <reading>おとな</reading>, grown up right in front of him.

ototoi.meaning_mnemonic: The smug goat is certain her one-contestant talent show already happened — she just can't recall which sun-window <kanji>day</kanji> it played in. She backs through yesterday's window, then one more window behind that, since in her world there is only ever <kanji>one</kanji> winner. Two windows back is where she finds it: the day before yesterday.
ototoi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a scruffy otter drags the same battered toy from the water, swearing it's the first time. The other otters know better — they watched that toy sink two mornings back, on <reading>おととい</reading>, and nobody tells the <reading>otter</reading> <reading>toy</reading> story twice.

otousan.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, red-faced and sweating under the noon sun, a father hauls a stalled cart the last hundred meters by rope while his kid cheers from beside the lone vending machine. That's the picture pinned to father, polite: the dad you'd point out respectfully to a stranger, not the tired grumble you'd use at home.
otousan.reading_mnemonic: As he heaves the cart past the vending machine, the kid shouts the word for him, and it lands in your ear as <reading>oh, tow, sun</reading> — dad towing, sun blazing overhead — the same beats as <reading>おとうさん</reading>. That's the polite word for pointing him out to a stranger on the trail, not the plain one for talking about your own.
otousan.description: お父さん (otousan) is the polite, respectful word for father — what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father in conversation. It contrasts with the plain 父 (chichi), which you use only when talking about your own father to people outside the family.

otouto.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the pesky little brother who trails you everywhere, small enough that shopkeepers assume he's still in diapers, always demanding you carry him piggyback until your arms give out. That exact whiny, tag-along presence is what points straight at a younger brother.
otouto.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the small brother stomps on the same customer's foot twice reaching for onigiri, and the customer yelps <reading>oh, toe, toe</reading> each time. The beeping till clerk sighs and says it again, plain: <reading>おとうと</reading>, always causing trouble.

otto.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman is washing laundry when her husband wades in fully dressed, chasing a sock that floated loose, soaking his only good shirt in the process. She doesn't even look up — of course that's who waded in after one sock, nobody else would bother. That reliable, faintly ridiculous devotion is (my) husband.
otto.reading_mnemonic: He climbs out of the river dripping head to toe, sock triumphantly in hand, and she just sighs, <reading>Otto</reading>, not again — the exact sound of <reading>おっと</reading>, her name for the husband who always wades in after the laundry.
otto.description: 夫 is the plain way a wife refers to her own husband when speaking to other people — not a word she'd use to call out to him directly, and not used for someone else's husband.

pan.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer grabs the last loaf off the shelf right as the till starts beeping, panicking because the shelf is otherwise all onigiri. He hugs it like it's the only bread left in Japan, mutters thanks under the fluorescent lights, and pays before anyone else spots it.
pan.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read: <reading>パン</reading>, borrowed straight from Portuguese pão — no derivation needed.

raigetsu.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads still waves in every traveler for shade, but tonight it's packed solid. It points up at the crescent overhead and tells the next pair to <kanji>come</kanji> back once that sliver of <kanji>month</kanji> has swung all the way around and grown thin again. That's next month's shade, not this one's.
raigetsu.reading_mnemonic: 来 already gives you らい and 月 already gives you げつ — stack them straight through into <reading>らいげつ</reading>.

rainen.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads waves its branches at the scarecrow, telling it to <kanji>come</kanji> rest in the shade. The scarecrow yells back that it has to stand in the field for the rest of the <kanji>year</kanji>, but promises to finally take a break next year.
rainen.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly what you learned for the kanji: 来 (らい) plus 年 (ねん) makes <reading>らいねん</reading>.

raishuu.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads is still waving <kanji>come</kanji> at anyone nearby, but now it's leaning off the far edge of the calendar page, calling toward the square just past the current loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> — beckoning travelers to a loop that hasn't even started. Next week.
raishuu.reading_mnemonic: 来 already carries the らい reading and 週 already carries the しゅう reading, so stacked together in order they simply give you <reading>らいしゅう</reading> — no story needed.

rei.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a ranger posts an official notice board each morning with the exact temperature. One frost-bitten dawn, the mercury refuses to rise past the middle line at all, and the ranger stamps the report with one stiff, formal number before trudging back down. That number is zero.
rei.reading_mnemonic: The ranger reading the thermometer is named Ray, and he announces temperatures stiffly, formally, no contractions ever. He reads the number in one clipped word, <reading>れい</reading> — <reading>Ray</reading> only sounds this formal when the mercury freezes at zero.
rei.description: 零 is the formal, written register for zero — the word you'd see on an official temperature report or hear in a stiff announcement, not the one you'd use casually reading out a phone number or a game score.

roku-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, eight cats are sprawled across the mossy steps at dawn. She sets the heavy iron offering lid down with a clang right on the top step, and two cats bolt at the sound, tails high. What's left staring up at the enormous bell is <kanji>six</kanji> cats, thoroughly unimpressed by the racket. The lid on top of eight, as always, leaves <kanji>six</kanji>.
roku-v.reading_mnemonic: 六's reading here is just the number's own reading you already learned: <reading>ろく</reading>.

sakana.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman casts his line for hours and reels in nothing but weeds, until a sudden tug nearly drags him into the water — he hauls back to find something flopping on the bank, gasping right alongside him. That flopping, gasping catch is the entire reason anyone stands at a riverbank all afternoon: fish.
sakana.reading_mnemonic: The fisherwoman working that same riverbank, <reading>Sock Anna</reading>, wades in after a lost sock and something latches onto her bare foot instead of the fabric — she yelps out the same sound as her own name, <reading>さかな</reading>, and from then on that's just the word for fish.

san-v.meaning_mnemonic: A teacher taps a chalk pointer against three stacked lines on the board, one, two, three, and by the third tap the class already knows what word is coming before she says it. There is no trick to uncover here: <kanji>three</kanji> lines stacked in a character just spells the word three, plainly, the way it has all along.
san-v.reading_mnemonic: 三 alone already reads <reading>さん</reading>, the same reading you counted out tapping the three lines.

seito.meaning_mnemonic: That same patch of earth where a seed splits open into <kanji>life</kanji> now stretches out as a schoolyard, planted with row after row of identical green shoots, all still too short to see over the fence. They're not finished yet — still rooted, still waiting their turn to grow — and that half-grown state is exactly what a pupil is.
seito.reading_mnemonic: At the school, a mob of first-years shuffles so close behind <reading>Sei</reading> that they keep landing on her <reading>toe</reading> — "say... toe!" she yelps each time. The name sticks: these tagalong underclassmen following the star student's every step become known as 「<reading>せいと</reading>」.

sen-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine's price display multiplies without warning: one bold slash scratches straight across the readout, the same slash that once capped that plus-sign cross into something bigger, and the number keeps climbing past every digit until it locks on one round <kanji>thousand</kanji> and finally stops beeping.
sen-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 千 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>せん</reading>.

sengetsu.meaning_mnemonic: Those two legs, already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone, are long gone before you've even reached the door. By the time you catch up, the sliver of <kanji>month</kanji> they left under has faded to nothing and grown back new. Whatever they did, they did it under last month's crescent.
sengetsu.reading_mnemonic: 先 already gives you せん and 月 already gives you げつ — lay them end to end into <reading>せんげつ</reading>.

sensei.meaning_mnemonic: The legs that always stride out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone reach the classroom first, plant themselves at the front, and refuse to sit down. Beneath their feet is the same patch of ground where a seed cracks open into <kanji>life</kanji> — because this is the one person whose ideas take root in you and grow. That's a teacher.
sensei.reading_mnemonic: 先 gives せん and 生 supplies the same せい you know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student — stack them together and you get exactly 「<reading>せんせい</reading>」.

senshuu.meaning_mnemonic: Those <kanji>previous</kanji> legs are at it again, always a step ahead — they've already marched clear across the loop of the <kanji>week</kanji> on the calendar page and finished tracing it before you woke up. By the time you look at the grid, that loop is closed and cold. Last week.
senshuu.reading_mnemonic: 先 already carries the せん reading and 週 already carries the しゅう reading, so stacked together in order they simply give you <reading>せんしゅう</reading> — no story needed.

shi-num.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the same sealed box waits among the mossy steps, its trapped mouth still murmuring numbers into the corner. A cat swats it off the step and the lid cracks — the mouth peeks out just far enough to hiss a hushed <kanji>four</kanji> before a monk claps the lid shut, refusing to let it say the number again.
shi-num.reading_mnemonic: That hushed <reading>し</reading> is the same reading 四 already taught you — the clipped <reading>shh</reading> the monk uses to cut the mouth off mid-count.
shi-num.description: This reading of 四 sounds identical to a much darker word, so hospitals, hotels, and gift-givers avoid it — floor numbers, room numbers, and counted items switch to the other reading, よん, instead. Learn to recognize both, but default to よん when you're the one speaking.

shichi-num.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, the same bent-nail hook holds gym jerseys instead of coats. There's only one hook by the lockers, so seven players fresh off the field cram their jerseys onto it at once, the nail sagging nearly sideways under the pile. The coach counts before it gives way: <kanji>seven</kanji> jerseys, all balanced on one crooked hook.
shichi-num.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here keeps the reading you already learned for formal counting: <reading>しち</reading>.
shichi-num.description: しち is the older, more formal reading of 七 — used in compounds, in reading dates and times aloud, and in fixed set phrases. なな is generally preferred when counting items alone or aloud, since しち can be mistaken for the word for one in quick speech.

shuumatsu.meaning_mnemonic: You trace the winding path for the <kanji>week</kanji> until you run out of calendar page completely and your finger slips off the paper. Dropping off the edge of that grid lands you right in the weekend.
shuumatsu.reading_mnemonic: You spend your entire weekend at the riverbank scrubbing the mud out of your car's <reading>shoe mats</reading> (<reading>しゅうまつ</reading>). You wash them for two days straight, completely ruining your actual weekend.

sobo.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till goes quiet as an elderly woman counts her coins one by one. Koichi leans over to the new hire and says simply: that's my grandmother, in for her onigiri. No polite title, no fuss — just family, plain and direct, the way you describe your own grandmother to someone else.
sobo.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old woman mutters sew, bow, sew, bow while stitching ribbons onto scarves. A child mishears the rhythm as <reading>そぼ</reading>, the word for grandmother, and now everyone at the water's edge calls her the <reading>sew-bow</reading> lady who happens to be somebody's grandmother too.
sobo.description: 祖母 is how you refer to your own grandmother when speaking to someone outside the family — plain and humble, with no polite title attached. It isn't what you'd call her directly, or use for someone else's grandmother, both of which take an address term instead.

sochira.meaning_mnemonic: You're already at Koichi's till, practically leaning on the register, when you ask where the onigiri is. Koichi doesn't even look up — he just tilts his chin two feet toward the shelf you're basically touching and grunts the sound out, because when the thing you want is that close, all you need to say is that way.
sochira.reading_mnemonic: You already know そ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>そちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"so-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no twist to catch you out.

sofu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the old man who rings Grandma Kane's one enormous shrine bell every single morning, out of habit rather than faith, then complains for an hour that his arm hurts. That specific, grumbling, ritual-bound old man is exactly your grandfather.
sofu.reading_mnemonic: After ringing the enormous bell, the old man collapses onto the shrine steps and announces he's <reading>so full</reading> — of aches, not food. The cats ignore him as he mutters it again, <reading>そふ</reading>, and refuses to get up.

soko.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone drops a sandal mid-crossing and it snags on a rock partway across the water. You point at the exact spot from the near bank, arm out straight, calling out to the person wading in: there, there, no, THERE — the sandal never moves, but your pointing finger fixes the place for good.
soko.reading_mnemonic: そこ is written entirely in kana the way it sounds, with no kanji standing behind it — you read <reading>そこ</reading> exactly as it's spelled.

sonna.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat knocks the enormous bell clean off its stand, and when she's told it was an accident she just stares at the wreckage — that kind of excuse, the kind aimed right back at whoever just spoke, never quite convincing her.
sonna.reading_mnemonic: Like its cousins, this word is pure kana, so <reading>そんな</reading> is pronounced exactly as spelled, with nothing underneath to decode.

sono.meaning_mnemonic: Your friend is squatting on the riverbank with three soaked shoes lined up beside them, and you are holding a sonar gun that refuses to lock onto anything near you. It only pings at objects sitting next to somebody else, whining so-no, so-no as it swings toward them. Whatever it picks out is that shoe, that bucket, that dripping thing over by your friend.
sono.reading_mnemonic: No decoding needed: this word is spelled in kana precisely as it is pronounced, <reading>その</reading>.
sono.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something in the listener's zone rather than yours, so a thing in their hand or on their side of the table takes this word even where English would say this. It also picks up something the other person has just mentioned, with nothing visible to point at.

sore.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer holds an onigiri up under your nose, and your pointing finger is so sore from a full shift at the beeping till that you can barely straighten it. You waggle the sore finger at the rice ball sitting there in his hands and grunt. Whatever is over by him, close enough for him to touch — that one.
sore.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>それ</reading>, so there is no reading to decode.
sore.description: Points at something near the person you are talking to, rather than near you — the middle rung of the near, middle, far set. It stands alone as a pronoun, so it never sits directly in front of a noun; the form that does that is a separate word.

suiyoubi.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>weekday</kanji>, you stand by the riverbank to watch the <kanji>sun</kanji> come up, but today a massive geyser of freezing <kanji>water</kanji> blasts out of the river and knocks you flat into the mud. You scrape yourself off, remembering that this mid-week flood always happens on Wednesday.
suiyoubi.reading_mnemonic: There are no new sounds to learn here, just combine the kanji readings you already know into <reading>すいようび</reading>.

tabemono.meaning_mnemonic: That tent pitched over a heaped tray — the shelter you duck into when you're hungry — gets dragged whole onto Sei's school sports field for a picnic, roof and all. The whole team ducks under it at once, and every dish sitting under that roof, from the rice down to the last pickle, gets <kanji>eaten</kanji> before the bell rings. Anything that ends up under that tent is, simply, food.
tabemono.reading_mnemonic: Every lunch break, a scrawny transfer student named <reading>Toby Moreno</reading> materializes at Koichi's konbini and buys out the entire onigiri shelf without saying a word. The clerk has started calling out <reading>たべもの</reading> the second the bell rings, because that name and that hunger always arrive together.

tamago.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the delivery truck arrives before dawn and unloads crate after crate of impossibly round, pale ovals, still warm from the truck's engine. Koichi holds one to the fluorescent light, taps it once, and it cracks open — bright yolk sliding across the counter: egg.
tamago.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the fat shrine cat curls into the offering bowl every morning. Someone finally claps and shouts <reading>Tama, go!</reading> — it slinks off, revealing one warm egg underneath. That shout is the reading: <reading>たまご</reading>.

te-v.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> is still hanging out mid-air, wrist and all, waiting for the shake nobody's ever finished. It doesn't close, it doesn't wave — it just stays there, open-palmed, being exactly the shape it always was. That patient, unshaken shape is the word for hand.
te-v.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same lesson: 手 already gave you two readings, and this word just borrows the plain <reading>て</reading> reading straight off it.

tomodachi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stranger reaches for the last onigiri the exact moment you do. Neither of you lets go. You end up splitting it on the curb outside, silent and suspicious of each other, until one bite in you're both laughing about it — and just like that, you've made a friend.
tomodachi.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a boy named <reading>Tomo</reading> won't cross the water without his small <reading>dachshund</reading> tucked under one arm. The two go everywhere together, so the locals just call the pair 「<reading>ともだち</reading>」 — one word for two creatures who refuse to be apart.

too.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, someone has arranged the onigiri into a stack of perfect crosses — the <kanji>ten</kanji> mark hikers make with two raised hands when they reach a full count. There are ten of them lined up by the register, each shaped like that same cross, and the till beeps once for every single one as the clerk recounts them. Ten things, stacked in crosses at the counter.
too.reading_mnemonic: This word is just 十's kun'yomi reading standing alone as the number word for ten things: 「<reading>とお</reading>」.

tooka.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and finds you at the shrine steps, raising both hands a little higher than yesterday, palms open like the <kanji>ten</kanji>-shaped cross you make once all your fingers are up. Nine sunrises of half-raised hands pass before the tenth, when both hands finally form that perfect cross overhead — ten days of raising, and it's the tenth.
tooka.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat keeps shoving the same toy car down all ten mossy steps, and it lands on your <reading>toe</reading> every single time. <reading>とおか</reading>, right on the toe, ten steps down — ten days of bruises later, you finally admit that's the sound of the tenth.

tsuitachi.meaning_mnemonic: The smug goat's one-contestant talent show — one stage, one prize, one judge, all her — only ever opens the instant the sun first climbs through the windowed frame of a brand new <kanji>day</kanji>. She refuses to be anything but <kanji>one</kanji>, so she insists on staging it the very moment each month's sun rises for the first time, never later. That stubborn need to go first, first day, every single month: the 1st.
tsuitachi.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane opens the shrine on the very first morning of the month and finds her legs unbearably <reading>too itchy</reading> — poison ivy from clearing the mossy steps. She scratches through the whole ceremony, grumbling that the reading for this day, <reading>ついたち</reading>, always shows up with an itch she can't shake.

tsuma.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a man climbs the mossy steps every evening expecting to be first, and every evening his own wife is already there ahead of him, feeding the shrine cats without a word of announcement. He never has to ask where she is — she is simply, quietly, always a step ahead of him. That settled certainty is (my) wife.
tsuma.reading_mnemonic: He calls up the steps, <reading>Sue, ma!</reading>, thinking he's found Grandma Kane — but it's his own wife who turns around, cat in her arms. That startled beat is the sound of <reading>つま</reading>: realizing, again, that his wife got there first.
tsuma.description: 妻 is the plain, slightly formal way a man refers to his own wife when talking to other people — it is not a word used for someone else's wife, and not one he'd use calling out to her directly.

watashi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tanuki knocks over the shiny new security mirror by the till and freezes, nose to nose with itself. It taps the glass, tilts its head, and decides, flatly, that the animal staring back must be the most important customer in the store: itself. From then on it restocks the onigiri shelf for nobody else, certain of exactly who it means when it talks about I.
watashi.reading_mnemonic: The tanuki taps the glass and gasps at what it sees — <reading>what a shiny</reading> creature — then realizes it's only its own reflection, saying <reading>わたし</reading>, I, over and over, delighted that the shiniest thing in the konbini turned out to be itself.

watashitachi.meaning_mnemonic: On the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat rings the enormous bell and every other cat in the place mobs the sound, wedging in shoulder to shoulder until they're one solid, purring mass on the step. Ask any single cat its name and the whole pile answers at once, because as far as they're concerned there's no such thing as one cat here anymore, only the pile. That fused, shoulder-to-shoulder answer is the meaning you want: we.
watashitachi.reading_mnemonic: Try to pet just one cat in the pile and the whole mass yowls back what sounds like <reading>what a she, touchy</reading> bunch — really the cats shouting <reading>わたしたち</reading>, we, in one voice, refusing to be split apart even for the bell.

yasai.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning Grandma Kane sets a fresh offering on the shrine steps, but this time it isn't rice or dried fish — it's a heap of raw produce, and the shrine cats sniff it once, turn their tails up, and stalk off toward the bell instead. Not even a temple cat will touch it. That offering nobody at the shrine wants is vegetables.
yasai.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane just sighs, '<reading>ya, sigh</reading>,' every single time the cats reject her offering and slink away, and that resigned little sigh is almost exactly the sound of <reading>やさい</reading> — the vegetables piled up on the shrine steps that nobody wants.

yattsu.meaning_mnemonic: At the base of the mountain trail, two hikers' legs split wider with every step up the steep slope, spreading apart like the shape of the number <kanji>eight</kanji> itself. By the vending machine at the top, you count the pairs of boots left behind by exhausted climbers: eight things, scattered where the trail finally levels out.
yattsu.reading_mnemonic: 八 reads やっ here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>やっつ</reading>」.

yokka.meaning_mnemonic: Trapped inside the enclosure, the mouth keeps counting under its breath, and on the try that decides everything it finally lands on <kanji>four</kanji>. The instant it shouts the number, the window's bar snaps back and the <kanji>sun</kanji> pours through into a brand new <kanji>day</kanji>. Four counted breaths, one sunrise — that's the 4th, four days gone.
yokka.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the onigiri shelf is stocked with egg yolks instead of rice this morning. He counts them rolling off one by one — one, two, three — and on the <reading>yolk</reading> that nearly hits the floor he calls out <reading>よっか</reading>, the fourth yolk saved just before day four's shift ends.

yon-v.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini sits that same sealed box, the mouth still trapped inside counting onigiri through the glass. Tonight it's a slow delivery — one, two, three — and on the next rice ball the mouth presses flat against the glass and stops. That flattened stare is the number stamped on this word: <kanji>four</kanji>.
yon-v.reading_mnemonic: Nothing to derive here — 四 already taught you the <reading>よん</reading> reading, the same stretch you reach for right before a big <reading>yawn</reading>.

yoru.meaning_mnemonic: Every cat in the neighborhood gathers on Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps only once the enormous bell has gone silent and the sky has turned fully black, packed shoulder to shoulder in a way they'd never risk in daylight. That one pitch-dark hour when they finally show themselves is the only word for it: night.
yoru.reading_mnemonic: The oldest cat on those steps is known only as <reading>Yore</reading> — legend has it she's kept watch since days of <reading>yore</reading>, though nobody living has ever actually seen her arrive. She only appears once <reading>よる</reading> falls, prowling the shrine in total dark before vanishing again by sunrise.

yottsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the trapped <kanji>four</kanji> mouth from inside the enclosure has escaped into the stockroom and wedged itself into a cardboard case behind the counter, still muttering its count under its breath. Koichi hauls the case onto the shelf and counts what's rattling around inside: four onigiri, no more, no less. Four things, sealed in one box.
yottsu.reading_mnemonic: 四 already carries the reading <reading>よっ</reading>, and つ stays つ, giving you exactly <reading>よっつ</reading> — four things, straight from readings you already know.

youka.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and lights the same crack in the riverbank ice — a crack shaped exactly like the splitting legs of <kanji>eight</kanji>. Each sunrise splits it wider: one, two, three, all the way to the eighth. By the eighth sunrise the ice has split clean into two drifting halves, eight days of widening, and it's officially the eighth.
youka.reading_mnemonic: A yoga instructor greets every sunrise with a pose that curls her spine into two loops, exactly like the number eight. She names this ritual her <reading>yoga</reading> day, and said quickly in Japanese it comes out as <reading>ようか</reading> — the 8th, eight days of practice in.

yuugata.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the enormous bell only rings once the light turns orange and the mossy steps fill with cats — never at noon, never after full dark, only in that hinge between day and night. That one ring marks evening arriving, gonged out over a hundred cats who all seem to expect it.
yuugata.reading_mnemonic: Every dusk the shrine cats surround Grandma Kane and yowl what sounds exactly like <reading>you got a</reading> curfew, and it's true: the bell tolls <reading>ゆうがた</reading> the moment the sky goes orange, and every cat scatters home for the night.

zero.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the team spends the entire match slipping on the wet grass, missing every shot, while the goalkeeper falls asleep against the post. The final whistle blows, the scoreboard locks in one flat, humiliating number, and the whole bench stares at it in silence. That number is zero.
zero.reading_mnemonic: ゼロ is spelled exactly the way it sounds — read the katakana <reading>ゼロ</reading> straight through, no hidden reading to dig for.
zero.description: ゼロ is the everyday spoken form, heard in scores, phone numbers, and casual temperature talk; formal or written contexts often reach for a different, more formal word instead.
